paragraphs.text: Before you begin
Moses Afolabi • Illustrated study edition • 2026

Read the whole Bible passage before working through a chapter. Scripture quotations use the King James Version. Modern application scenes and illustrations are teaching examples. They do not describe documented events or verified personal testimonies.
Historical accounts are identified and accompanied by source links. Consider their particular setting as you reflect on the biblical passage.

Take time to read the explanation, study the visual summary, and complete the practice in your own notebook. Discuss difficult questions with a trusted pastor or mature believer. Return to the chapter after trying its suggested action.
The PDF contains still illustrations. The separate animated companion adds gentle motion and chapter prompts.

Chapter 1 Blessed in Christ
Begin with what God gives in Christ. Gratitude can steady the heart while you take responsibility for the day.
Read Ephesians 1:1–6, Luke 19:1–10, and 2 Corinthians 5:17–21. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.
God is the giver
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ: — Ephesians 1:3
Paul begins with praise to God. Trace the sentence. The God and Father of Jesus

Christ acts. Believers receive. The blessings are spiritual, and Paul locates them in Christ . In the following verses he names adoption, acceptance, redemption, forgiveness, and the promised Holy Spirit. Those are the kinds of gifts the opening blessing leads you to look for. If you read verse 3 on a discouraging day, continue through the paragraph and name one of the gifts in Paul’s words. A verse about spiritual blessing becomes more concrete when its next sentences tell you what the blessing consists of.

A believer’s circumstances can change rapidly. Work may go well for months and then a mistake may become public. A friend may welcome you in one season and misunderstand you in the next. The movement of Paul’s opening sentence gives you a different starting point for handling these experiences. Ask what God says He has done in Christ. Then ask what the situation requires of you. Receiving a correction and accepting God’s grace can happen in the same conversation.
Chosen for a life that reflects God
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: — Ephesians 1:4

Paul connects God’s purpose with holiness. The words “that we should be” give a direction for the life that follows. When you study identity in Christ, ask where a gift leads. Belonging to God calls a person to conduct that reflects Him. At home, that might mean admitting you promised to be available and then failed to follow through. At work, it could mean correcting a detail that benefited you but misled someone else. Make the example concrete enough to distinguish a faithful action from a good intention.

Notice where Paul places the foundation. God’s purpose precedes the believer’s first opportunity to prove anything. That order matters when you receive criticism. You can hear what is true, acknowledge any harm, and decide what a repair will require. You can also pray for strength to do it without making the person’s approval the final measure of your relationship with God.
To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved. — Ephesians 1:6

Paul concludes this movement of praise by speaking of grace and acceptance in the Beloved. Read verses 3 and 6 together. Which words identify God’s action? Which words locate that action in Christ? Which words name the purpose of praise? These questions keep the study close to the passage and give you language you can use in prayer.
Scriptural testimony · Zacchaeus receives Jesus and makes amends
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold. — Luke 19:8

In Luke 19, Jesus calls Zacchaeus by name and tells him He will stay at his house. Zacchaeus receives Him joyfully. The people grumble because Jesus has gone to be a guest of a man they regard as a sinner. Zacchaeus then speaks about giving and restoration, and Jesus declares that salvation has come to the house. Read the whole sequence slowly. Note what Jesus does first and what Zacchaeus says about money afterward.

Zacchaeus’s story helps you consider the connection between relationship and action in Ephesians 1:3–6. Grace can reach the very thing a person has tried to protect. A person who benefited from a misleading financial record can name the record, correct the total, and speak to the person affected. If a repair involves other people or a formal process, work with the people responsible and respect the needs of those harmed.
Historical testimony · John Newton and the cost of facing the truth

John Newton experienced a severe storm at sea in 1748, an event he associated with a turn in his spiritual life. He continued in the slave trade afterward, including as a captain of slave ships. Decades later, as a minister, he published Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade in 1788. He publicly acknowledged his participation and used what he knew to expose the trade.

The timeline matters. Newton’s spiritual awakening did not immediately bring him to acknowledge the wrong he was doing to enslaved Africans and their families. His later testimony can help a reader take a hard look at areas in which they have long accepted an unjust practice. It also directs attention to the people who bore the harm. Admiration for a public figure’s eventual change can never by itself address what was done. A truthful account names the wrong, listens to affected people, and considers what responsibility belongs to those who benefited.

Read Ephesians 1:4 again after considering the history. Paul’s words about holiness give believers a reason to let God’s truth challenge practices that once felt ordinary. Ask which part of your life you readily bring under the teaching of Christ and which part you tend to excuse. Cowper & Newton Museum, John Newton: Early Life and the Slave Trade
Worked example · Take responsibility without losing your footing

Consider a fictional project leader in Accra who promised a customer a delivery date before the team confirmed it. The schedule slipped. The leader can write three sentences: “I promised Friday without checking with the people who do the work. In Christ, God has given me grace and called me to live truthfully. I will verify the next date with the team and explain the error to the customer.” Each sentence does a different job. The first tells the truth about the event. The second names the foundation for the response. The third identifies a repair another person can recognize.

Study and application
1. Write verse 3 in your own words. Keep God as the giver and Christ as the One in whom the blessing is received.
2. Read verses 4 and 6 together. Describe how holiness and grace are connected in the paragraph.
3. Name one recent criticism or setback. Write one sentence about what happened and one sentence about what God says in the passage.
4. Select an action someone else could observe. If you need to make a correction, write who needs to hear it and when.
5. Revisit the exercise after a week. Record whether your response changed and what still needs attention.

Prayer. Father, thank You for what You have given us in Jesus Christ. Let Your Word teach me where I belong. Give me humility to face what needs correcting and courage to make amends where I can. Help me serve others with gratitude for Your grace. Amen.
Chapter 2 Adopted Through Jesus Christ
Belonging takes visible form through patient attention, welcome, and shared life in the household of faith.
Read Ephesians 1:3–6, Romans 8:14–17, and Galatians 4:4–7.

In Ephesians 1:5, adoption is something God purposes and brings about through Jesus Christ. The language is about belonging and relationship. Paul joins it to the praise of God’s grace in the next verse. When you see those ideas together, you can ask which comes first in your own thinking. Do you wait until you have performed well to approach God, or do you draw near through Christ and bring your life as it is into that relationship?

Romans 8 adds that believers have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom they cry, “Abba, Father.” Paul places that cry alongside the Spirit’s witness and the language of inheritance. Galatians 4 ties the same relationship to the sending of the Son and the sending of His Spirit. Read the passages together and identify the actions God takes. The gift of belonging gives the believer a reason to pray, obey, and mature.
Recognize the habits of someone who expects to be sent away

A new member of a congregation in Lagos has become generous with his time. He volunteers whenever there is a need but becomes anxious whenever he declines a request. He fears losing his place among the people. He can review that habit in the light of Ephesians. If God has brought him into His family through Christ, what would it look like to serve freely? A practical beginning may be to accept one responsibility he can keep, thank God for the opportunity, and tell the team when he is unavailable.

Adoption language can also be difficult for people who carry painful memories of family. Read Paul’s description from the direction he gives it. Begin with what God has done through Jesus. Let Scripture teach you how the Father receives you. If an association makes it hard to pray, start with the words of Ephesians 1:5 and speak one honest sentence to God about that difficulty.
What the Father has done through the Son
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, — Ephesians 1:5, KJV

Read the sentence with verse 6. Paul names the relationship God intends, the One through whom it comes, and the grace it displays. The phrase “to himself” gives direction to the adoption. God receives people into relationship with Himself through Jesus Christ. A reader who feels driven to earn approval can pause at each phrase. Ask what action the verse assigns to God and what reason the verse gives for that action. Keep your answer tied to what Paul says before you describe what you feel.

The use of adoption language also draws attention to the family believers enter. A person may rightly rejoice that the Father receives them, then struggle to receive a believer whose background is unfamiliar. Read the plural pronoun carefully. Paul speaks of us . If you have received a place in God’s household through the Son, consider one concrete way to make another member welcome. Explain a custom a newcomer may not understand or introduce them to someone who can answer their question.
The Spirit gives believers words to address the Father
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. — Galatians 4:6, KJV

Trace the two sendings in Galatians 4:4–7. God sends His Son, who redeems those under the law so they may receive adoption. God sends the Spirit of His Son into their hearts. The order helps you understand the cry of verse 6. Believers have grounds to address God as Father because of what God has done through His Son. If your prayer feels awkward, begin with the relationship the passage describes and make one request in your ordinary voice.

Romans places the same cry alongside the Spirit’s witness and inheritance. Read all the way into Romans 8:17. Paul speaks of suffering with Christ as well as glory with Him. That context helps a believer facing a hard week. Difficult circumstances can be a place to address the Father and seek His help. Bring the difficulty into prayer as it is. If your family has received unwelcome news, ask for what each person needs to face the next decision, the next conversation, or the next day.
Scriptural testimony · The father goes out to his sons
And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. — Luke 15:31, KJV

Read Luke 15:11–32. The younger son returns with a confession. The father welcomes him and orders a celebration. The elder brother, though close to home, speaks of his service and resents the celebration. The father goes out and reasons with him too. Pay attention to whom the father addresses and what he tells each son. The story can expose the habit of treating years of service as an argument against mercy for someone else.

Luke’s parable and Paul’s teaching serve different purposes. Use Luke to consider the joy of receiving a person who returns, and use Ephesians and Galatians to explain how adoption comes through Christ. In a congregation, these passages may lead you to welcome someone who has been away for a long time. A sincere invitation, a place to sit, and a chance to speak privately can help them return without being expected to explain their whole life at once.
Historical testimony · Augustine prepares for baptism

In Confessions , Augustine gives an account of his struggle before conversion. In Book VIII he describes hearing words that prompted him to take up and read. He opens Paul’s letter to the Romans and reads the closing verses of Romans 13. Book IX describes his withdrawal from the teaching position he had held and his preparation for baptism. He records being baptized along with his friend Alypius and his son Adeodatus.

Read this as Augustine’s account of his own life. It gives a historical illustration of how reading Scripture, responding to conviction, and entering the life of a Christian community can belong to one movement. His circumstances differ from yours. Ask which part of your own response needs attention. You might open Scripture with another believer, speak to a pastor about baptism, or make a change that allows you to keep a commitment you have been postponing. Augustine, Confessions, Books VIII–IX, Christian Classics Ethereal Library

Practice belonging in a relationship
- In Ephesians, mark through Jesus Christ . In Galatians, mark each place where God sends someone. What does each action make possible?
- Write one task you do mainly because you fear rejection. Name one way you could approach that task as a person who belongs to God.

Choose a responsibility you take on mainly because you fear losing approval. Identify the part you can offer gladly and the part that would exceed your commitments. Write a sentence to the person who needs to know. End by praying Galatians 4:6 in your own words. After the conversation, record what you were able to offer and whether your fear accurately predicted the other person’s response.

Prayer. Father, thank You for receiving me through Jesus Christ. Teach me to respond to Your grace with honest prayer and willing service. Help me recognize the people around me as brothers and sisters who also depend on Your grace. Amen.
Chapter 3 Redeemed and Forgiven
Grace gives courage to tell the truth. A sincere apology names the harm and makes room for a fitting repair.
Read Ephesians 1:7–10, Ephesians 4:31–32, and 1 John 1:8–9.

Paul sets redemption and forgiveness together in Ephesians 1:7. Redemption speaks of release secured through Christ. Paul names His blood and then speaks of the riches of God’s grace. The passage asks you to consider the cost Christ bore and the generosity of the God who grants forgiveness. Slow down here. Name the wrongdoing honestly while also reading what the verse says about the provision for it.

There are two particularly unhelpful ways to respond to failure. One is to smooth away the details until there is nothing left to admit. The other is to replay the incident long after you have confessed it, as if more distress will give you a different standing with God. First John gives believers something concrete to do. Confess the sin and trust God’s character. Where another person was harmed, ask what repair you can reasonably make.
Work through the response after a real wrong

A team member in São Paulo took credit for work another person contributed. She was praised in front of the group and realized she had allowed the mistaken impression to continue. At home she confessed what she did to God. The next day she named the contribution openly and spoke privately with her coworker. She made a truthful correction in the same setting where people received the original impression.

For an incident of your own, separate three statements. Write what happened. Write what Christ’s work means for a believer who confesses sin. Then write the next faithful action. Some situations require an apology, repayment, or a conversation with an appropriate leader. Consider the safety and wishes of the people affected when deciding how to approach them.

Listen again to Ephesians 4:32. Paul connects a believer’s conduct toward others to God’s forgiveness in Christ. A person who has received mercy has a foundation for offering mercy while remaining truthful about harm. Take time to think where that connection is most difficult for you.
Follow the sentence from the cross to forgiveness
In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace; — Ephesians 1:7, KJV

The phrase “in whom” refers back to the Beloved in verse 6. Paul names the One in whom the gift is received, the means by which redemption comes, and the grace according to which forgiveness is given. Take each phrase in turn. Forgiveness is linked to the blood of Christ. The person confessing has something to look to beyond their own distress. Paul’s reference to riches places the emphasis on God’s generosity.

Read verses 8–10 too. Paul moves from grace toward God’s purpose of gathering all things in Christ. Personal forgiveness belongs within that larger purpose. A person can begin applying it in a narrow place, such as an apology to a coworker, while remembering that God’s work extends beyond the resolution of one dispute. The small repair is still worth making. It can make truth and mercy visible in the relationship where the wrong took place.
What confession says about the deed and about God
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Read 1 John 1:5–10. John contrasts walking in light with claiming to have no sin. Confession names conduct in the light of

God’s truth. It also relies on God’s faithfulness and justice. When a reader struggles to believe they can be forgiven, ask them to read the reason given in the verse. The text directs attention to God’s character rather than the intensity of the reader’s feelings.

Distinguish confession from a general statement of embarrassment. “I feel terrible about what happened” describes distress. “I showed another person your message without permission” identifies an action and gives the other person a clearer account of why an apology is needed. When a repair is possible, decide what has to change. You might ask recipients to respect privacy, correct a false impression, or step back from a responsibility while trust is restored.
Scriptural testimony · David faces what Nathan says
And David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the LORD. And Nathan said unto David, The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV

Read 2 Samuel 12:1–14. Nathan’s story stirs David’s judgment before Nathan identifies David as the man who has done wrong. David’s confession is brief and direct. Nathan’s response includes both pardon and consequences. Read Psalm 51 alongside the narrative. The prayer for a clean heart asks for change at the source of the conduct, while the surrounding story keeps readers mindful of the people harmed.

Ask whether you apply different explanations to the same conduct depending on who did it. You might call another person’s account misleading and describe your own as a mistake anyone could make. Write a statement you would accept as truthful from someone else. Then use the same standard for yourself.
Historical testimony · Corrie ten Boom remembers a request for forgiveness

In a first-person account originally published in 1972, Corrie ten Boom recalls meeting a former concentration camp guard after speaking about forgiveness in Munich in 1947. She recognized him from Ravensbrück, where her sister had died. She recounts that he approached her and asked for forgiveness. She describes the difficulty of responding and remembers praying for help before taking his hand.

Her account is one person’s testimony about one encounter after the war. It can help readers see why Ephesians 4:32 grounds the call to forgive in the forgiveness believers receive in Christ. Corrie’s account also gives room for the struggle that can accompany such a response. People dealing with ongoing harm may need protection, boundaries, and support. A person can consider forgiveness while still pursuing accountability and protecting those at risk. Corrie ten Boom, Guideposts Classics: Corrie ten Boom on Forgiveness

Workbook practice · Plan a repair that fits the harm

Write three sentences. Name the act plainly. Identify who was affected and what they lost or were led to believe. Describe the smallest truthful correction that would address the harm. If your words were public, consider who needs the correction. If harm is ongoing, stop the conduct and seek appropriate help before attempting a conversation.

Prayer. Father, thank You for redemption and forgiveness through Jesus Christ. I bring You what I have done in plain words. Lead me to make the repair I can make, and teach me to deal kindly and truthfully with the people around me. Amen.
Chapter 4 Sealed with the Holy Spirit
Return to the promise in its passage. Assurance grows as the gospel is heard, believed, and carried into conduct.
Read Ephesians 1:11–14, Ephesians 4:30–32, and Romans 8:15–16.

Trace the movement of Ephesians 1:13. Paul speaks of hearing the word of truth, believing in Christ, and being sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. The next verse calls the Spirit the earnest of the inheritance. The word earnest describes a pledge. Paul locates assurance in what God gives. He invites the believer to look beyond the changing emotions of an ordinary week toward the faithfulness of the One who has made the promise.

Ephesians 4:30 brings the same truth into the way believers treat each other. Paul speaks of the day of redemption and warns against grieving the Spirit. Nearby he warns against corrupt speech and urges kindness. Read both passages before applying the teaching. One paragraph gives assurance. The other gives concrete direction for the person who has received that assurance.
Bring the teaching into an ordinary week

A believer in Bangkok wakes up feeling spiritually dull after several nights of poor sleep. Later, an abrupt message from a coworker tempts her to send a sharp reply. She can read Ephesians 1 and thank God for His promise, then read Ephesians 4 and consider what would build up the person receiving the reply. She can ask a clarifying question and wait before pressing send. That small choice gives her a place to practice what she has read.

Make two notes when you study this chapter. Under God’s promise , summarize what Ephesians 1:13–14 says. Under my response , identify one action from Ephesians 4:29–32 to practice. Return to the notes on a day when you feel discouraged and on a day when you feel confident. Observe how the same Scripture addresses both days.
Follow hearing and believing through the sentence

In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, — Ephesians 1:13, KJV

Paul identifies what the believers heard. It was the word of truth, the gospel of their salvation. The sentence then speaks of believing and being sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. Read it in relation to the preceding words about hope in Christ. The Spirit’s presence is part of the saving work Paul praises God for. A reader seeking assurance can begin by asking whom the gospel directs them to trust.

Think about what hearing involves in an ordinary week. A believer may hear a sermon, read a paragraph in Ephesians, and then encounter an accusation or a setback that occupies the mind for the rest of the day. Returning to the text helps place that experience within a larger account. Read the whole sentence aloud and write what God has done. Then bring the unsettled feeling into prayer. The prayer can be sincere while the feeling is still unresolved.
Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory. — Ephesians 1:14, KJV

The word earnest names a pledge associated with what is to come. Paul’s language points forward to the completion of redemption. Read verses 13–14 together, then identify what is already given and what the passage still anticipates. The Spirit is given now, and the inheritance has a future fullness. Christian hope has room for both realities. This can strengthen a believer who is waiting through a season they cannot resolve by effort alone.
Scriptural testimony · The jailer hears the gospel
And they spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house. — Acts 16:32, KJV

Read Acts 16:25–34. The jailer asks Paul and Silas what he must do to be saved. They direct him to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, speak the word to the household, and the account goes on to describe care, baptism, and rejoicing. Notice the place of the spoken message in the narrative. The jailer receives an answer with a definite object of faith. The next actions show a changed relationship with the people who had been in his custody.

This testimony helps a reader move from a vague question about whether they feel different to the content of what they have heard and believed. Write one sentence about who Jesus is and one about what He has done. Use the passages you are studying to check your answer. Bring any unclear question to a mature believer who will read the text with you.
Let assurance reach your speech
And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. — Ephesians 4:30, KJV

Read Ephesians 4:25–32 as a connected paragraph. Paul speaks about truth, anger, work, speech, bitterness, kindness, and forgiveness. He places the warning about grieving the Spirit inside these instructions about daily relationships. When studying the seal in chapter 1, return to this paragraph to see what conduct fits the gift received. A person who belongs to God has reason to examine how their words affect another member of the body.

Consider a fictional team member in Nairobi who realizes a joke in a group chat humiliated a colleague. The immediate temptation is to say everyone is too sensitive. Reading Ephesians 4:29–30 gives a different question. Did the message build up the people who received it? The team member can acknowledge the effect, remove the message where possible, and apologize without demanding that the colleague make the situation comfortable.
Assurance can give courage for the correction.
Historical testimony · Wesley records assurance in Christ

John Wesley’s journal records an experience at a meeting in Aldersgate Street on May 24, 1738. He had been listening to a reading related to Luther’s preface to Romans. His account connects assurance of forgiveness with trust in Christ. The Museum of Methodism preserves and interprets this event as a significant moment in his life and ministry.

The testimony describes Wesley’s experience and the object of his trust. A reader can learn from the attention it gives to Christ while allowing their own emotions to have a different course. Read Ephesians 1:13 again and name the gospel Paul identifies as the word of truth. That gives a steady place from which to pray for understanding, seek counsel, and continue in faithful conduct. Museum of Methodism and John Wesley’s House, John Wesley’s Life

Workbook practice · Put promise beside conduct

Divide a page into two parts. In the first, write a sentence summarizing Ephesians 1:13–14. In the second, write a specific action from Ephesians 4:25–32 that needs attention this week. Pray over both. At the end of the week, record what you learned about God’s promise and what changed in your conduct toward someone else.

Prayer. Father, thank You for giving the promised Holy Spirit to those who believe in Christ. Give me steadiness when my feelings change. Let my words build people up, and teach me to act with the kindness I have received in Jesus. Amen.
Chapter 5 The Eyes of Your Understanding
Ask for understanding, then keep learning. Compare your first impression with the words and setting of the passage.
The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, — Ephesians 1:18, KJV

Read Ephesians 1:15–23. Paul has heard of the believers’ faith and love and thanks God for them. His prayer looks forward from what is already present. He wants them to perceive more clearly the hope of God’s call, the riches of His inheritance, and the greatness of His power. Verses 20–23 identify the resurrection and exaltation of Christ as the decisive example of that power. The prayer gives a believer a way to seek understanding when familiar words have stopped affecting how they see their circumstances.
Scriptural testimony · The road to Emmaus
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures, — Luke 24:45, KJV

Read Luke 24:13–35 and 44–49. The two disciples explain what they had hoped. Jesus takes them through Scripture. Later, with the gathered disciples, He opens their understanding. The chapter connects clearer sight to the Scriptures and to who Jesus is. If discouragement has narrowed your perspective, try reading the whole paragraph and asking how its subject is connected to the resurrection rather than treating one line as a promise of the outcome you already want.

Practice. Choose one phrase from Paul’s prayer. Write what it refers to in the paragraph, then turn it into a request for one person. Pray again after a week and record what you understand more clearly.
Name the hope Paul wants believers to know
That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: — Ephesians 1:17, KJV

Paul’s request concerns knowing God. Continue through verses 18–23 and list what he wants the believers to understand. The calling, inheritance, and power belong within a prayer directed to the Father. The final verses center the risen and exalted Christ. These details give you a way to study hope with its source in view. Ask what God has done and what future His action opens for His people.

A discouraging circumstance can become so large in your thoughts that you read every verse as a comment on that circumstance. Begin this prayer by letting Paul name its subject. Read the words about Christ’s resurrection before returning to the concern that brought you to the passage. You may still need to solve a practical problem, but you can approach it with a fuller picture of the Lord to whom you belong.
Scriptural testimony · Elisha’s servant sees more
And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. — 2 Kings 6:17, KJV, opening sentence

Read 2 Kings 6:8–23. The servant sees an army surrounding the city and asks what they can do. Elisha prays, and the servant sees the protection the narrative describes. Later the account moves toward the treatment of the captured soldiers. Follow that whole movement. The story concerns more than a moment of reassurance. It leads into decisions about people who had come as enemies.

Use the story alongside Ephesians with attention to their different settings. Elisha’s servant receives sight of a particular provision in a particular conflict. Paul asks believers to understand what God has accomplished in Christ. Both invite a reader to consider the limits of an immediate perception. When fear is making the whole decision, ask what relevant truth or information has been overlooked.

Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Practice a prayer that keeps learning

Choose a person facing an uncertain season. Ask their permission to remember them in prayer and learn what they would welcome you praying about. Then pray Ephesians 1:17–19 for them in your own words. Ask for knowledge of God, clearer hope, and an understanding of His power. Keep the person’s actual situation in view without supplying an outcome they never asked you to seek.

Over the next week, read one part of the prayer each day. On one day mark its verbs. On another, trace its references to Christ. On another, compare the opening thanksgiving with the requests. At the end of the week, explain the prayer aloud in a few sentences. Record one way the study changed what you asked for and one question you still need to explore.
Prayer. Father, open the eyes of my understanding. Teach me the hope of Your calling and let the risen Christ shape how I see these circumstances. Amen.
Chapter 6 Made Alive by Grace
Receive the new beginning God gives. Supportive fellowship can help you practice the next faithful response.
But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) — Ephesians 2:4–5, KJV

Read Ephesians 2:1–10. Paul moves from the old condition to God’s intervention. The words “But God” signal who acts and why. The passage names mercy, love, and grace before it calls attention to the works believers are created to do. In verse 5, quickened means made alive. Read the sentence with that meaning and notice that Paul says together with Christ . The new life comes through union with Him.
Scriptural testimony · Paul remembers the mercy he received
And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. — 1 Timothy 1:14, KJV

Read 1 Timothy 1:12–17 alongside Acts 9:1–19. Paul recalls his earlier conduct plainly and gives thanks for the mercy he received. In Acts, the encounter with Jesus changes the direction of his journey. He then receives help through Ananias. Grace can bring a person to recognize their need and receive the care of people they once resisted.

If an old way of living has become part of how you introduce yourself, read both accounts slowly. Make room for a truthful account of what you did and for an equally truthful account of the mercy you received.
Ask how your next action can show the direction in which you are now walking.

Practice. In two short paragraphs, describe what Ephesians says about life before God’s intervention and what it says God has done in Christ. End with one change a person close to you could recognize.
Hear grace and faith in the same sentence
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV

Paul identifies the source of salvation and the way believers receive it. Grace directs attention to God’s generosity. Faith directs attention to trust. The following warning about boasting shows why the order matters in relationships. If you speak about another person as though your better conduct made you more worthy of mercy, reread the sentence and identify what you received. Gratitude can change how you address someone who is only beginning to learn.

Read verse 10 after verses 8–9. Paul gives good works a purpose within the life God creates. Write one sentence about the gift and one sentence about the conduct that follows. This can help when you are tempted either to earn standing through busyness or to treat grace as a reason to postpone a clear responsibility. Ask what faithful action belongs to the person God has made alive.
Scriptural testimony · The younger son returns
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry. — Luke 15:24, KJV

Read Luke 15:11–24. The son comes to himself in a place of hunger, rehearses a confession, and returns. The father sees him, has compassion, and receives him. The father’s words about death and life give the celebration its reason. Pay attention to the relationship named in the sentence. The father calls him his son as he explains why the household is rejoicing.

Use the parable to consider the reception of a person who returns to a congregation after a long absence. Ask what welcome would make it possible for that person to take a next step. You may be able to offer a private conversation or an introduction to someone who can answer their questions. Give them room to tell their story at their own pace.
Visual summary
Mercy reaches the sinner
Life is received by grace
Faith responds to God
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Work through a new beginning

Consider a fictional student in Kumasi who has hidden a failed examination from her family. She is afraid that telling the truth will settle what everyone thinks of her. Reading Ephesians 2 gives her words for mercy and grace. It also gives her reason to act. She can explain the result, ask the school about the resit, and discuss a realistic study plan. The truthful conversation and the plan both belong to her response.

Choose a delayed responsibility of your own. Write what you have avoided, what information you need, and whom you should speak with. Pray over the list, then act on one item today. After the conversation, record the part that was difficult and the help you received. Return to the passage and give thanks for the mercy that made it possible to begin honestly.
Prayer. Father, thank You for Your rich mercy. Help me remember what You have done in Christ and live with gratitude today. Amen.
Chapter 7 Created for Good Works
Skill becomes service through attention to a real need. Useful good works can begin with what is already in your hands.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. — Ephesians 2:10, KJV

Read verses 8–10 as one unit. Good works have a clear place in Paul’s argument. God saves by grace through faith, and the life He gives has a purpose. The word “walk” suggests ordinary conduct over time. A person can begin with a faithful action that fits the needs of the people around them. A habit of reliable service can show what a larger promise means in practice.
Scriptural testimony · Dorcas serves with what she can make
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did. — Acts 9:36, KJV

Read Acts 9:36–43 and notice the detail in verse 39. Widows show Peter the garments Dorcas made while she was with them. The story gives tangible form to the phrase “good works.” Think of a skill you already have and a person who could use it. Ask what would help. A seamstress might mend a garment. A person who knows how to complete a form might sit with a neighbor while they read it.

Choose a commitment you can keep. Identify who can say what is needed, what you can provide, and when it would help. On the following week, ask whether the service was useful. The person receiving it can teach you how to do the work better.
Practice. Write one skill, one person or group with a practical need, and one task you can complete this week. Check that the task serves the need they described.
Read the gift before the calling
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV

The words immediately before verse 10 determine how you read workmanship and good works. Paul gives God the credit for salvation, then speaks of the life that follows. If service has become a way to settle whether you are accepted, return to the order of the paragraph. Thank God for His gift, then consider what help the people around you actually need. You may find that a smaller task done reliably serves them better than a public promise you cannot keep.

The word “walk” in verse 10 suggests conduct repeated over time. A person who helps a neighbor complete a difficult form can ask afterward which part was unclear. At the next visit, they can bring a clearer explanation. Good works can deepen as the person serving learns from the person receiving help. That learning is part of caring well.
Scriptural testimony · A need is organized responsibly
Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables. — Acts 6:2, KJV

Read Acts 6:1–7. A complaint concerns widows overlooked in daily provision. The apostles bring the matter to the disciples and give instructions for selecting people to oversee the work. The response takes the complaint seriously and assigns responsibility. Read the description of the people sought for the task. Practical service needs trustworthy judgment as well as willingness.

A congregation can learn from the sequence. Hear the complaint, identify the need, choose suitable people, and give them a defined responsibility. If you are offering help, ask whom you should report to and which information must remain private. If you coordinate the work, ask whether the people receiving provision have a clear way to raise a problem.
Visual summary
Created in Christ
Recognize a genuine need
Walk in good works
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Workbook project

Choose one task you can complete within a week. Write the need in the recipient’s words, the action you can take, and the time agreed. Check with the appropriate person before beginning. When the task is done, ask one practical question about whether it helped. Give thanks for the opportunity and record one improvement for the next time.
Prayer. Father, thank You that I am Your workmanship in Christ. Give me eyes to see a need and willingness to serve in a way that helps. Amen.
Chapter 8 Brought Near and Built Together
A welcome becomes credible when someone has room to participate. Ask the newcomer what would help them belong.
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. — Ephesians 2:13, KJV

Read Ephesians 2:11–22. Paul asks Gentile believers to remember how far off they once were. He locates their arrival in the work of Christ. In the next verses, Christ is the peace who makes the two one and reconciles them to God through the cross. The repeated images of citizenship, household, and building show the communal dimension of the passage. God gives people a place with others whom they may once have regarded as strangers.
Scriptural testimony · Peter enters the house of Cornelius
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: — Acts 10:34, KJV

Read Acts 10:28–48. Peter crosses a threshold he had previously understood as a barrier. He hears why Cornelius sent for him and then speaks about Jesus. The events challenge the assumptions Peter brought into the house. The story can guide a congregation that wants to make belonging visible. Ask someone new what they had to figure out on their own. Listen closely enough to learn whether the barrier was language, a physical entrance, an unfamiliar custom, or an assumption that everyone already knew someone.

Practice. Draw a simple route from a first visit to a meaningful conversation. Mark where a person might lose their way. Ask one newcomer or host to check your assumption and choose a change you can make together.
One household takes shape in daily conduct
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; — Ephesians 2:19, KJV

Paul gives several images for belonging in Ephesians 2:19–22. Citizenship concerns a shared standing. Household language concerns a place with others. Building language describes people joined together into a dwelling for God through the Spirit. Read each picture and ask what responsibility it creates toward another believer. A household member can notice when someone is missing information that the familiar members take for granted.

Consider a newcomer in a congregation where announcements switch between two languages. Someone who speaks both can summarize the practical details and ask which parts need translation. The need may be small enough to miss and important enough to determine whether the person returns. Belonging becomes visible through the attention the community gives to such details.
Scriptural testimony · A welcome is tested
But Barnabas took him, and brought him to
the apostles, and declared unto them how he had seen the Lord in the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how he had preached boldly at Damascus in the name of Jesus. — Acts 9:27, KJV

Read Acts 9:26–30. The disciples are afraid of Saul because of what they know of his earlier conduct. Barnabas helps by giving an account of Saul’s encounter with the Lord and his ministry. The story includes both understandable fear and a person who can provide relevant testimony. Welcoming someone can involve truthful information and responsible introductions.

If a new person wants to serve, learn what preparation and oversight the role requires. A warm welcome and appropriate procedures can work together. Explain the next steps plainly so the person can understand how to participate. A leader can also identify someone who will answer questions through the process.
Visual summary
Brought near through Christ
Share access to the Father
Build a household of faith
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Practice a welcome from the visitor’s side

Walk through your congregation’s arrival route as a first-time visitor would. Note where the room, time, or next action is unclear. Ask someone who recently joined whether your observations match their experience. Choose one change you can make with the people responsible. After trying it, ask whether it helped. Read Ephesians 2:19 again and pray for the person whose experience taught you something.
Prayer. Father, thank You for bringing us near through Christ. Show me how to treat people as members of a household You are building together. Amen.
Chapter 9 Strengthened in the Inner Person
Inner strength can appear as a quiet act of endurance. Ask for grace to fulfill one responsibility before you.
That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man; — Ephesians 3:16, KJV

Read Ephesians 3:14–21. Paul bows his knees before the Father and asks for strength through the Spirit. The following verse connects the request with Christ dwelling in believers’ hearts by faith. Paul’s prayer addresses the person who has to live through a circumstance. It gives believers a way to seek God’s help for patience, faithful speech, and endurance in the middle of an unresolved responsibility.
Scriptural testimony · Paul receives grace in weakness
And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV, first sentence

Read 2 Corinthians 12:7–10. Paul repeatedly asks for the thorn to depart. The answer he records gives him language for strength in weakness. Hold the request and the answer together. You can ask for a burden to be removed and also ask for what you need to live faithfully while it remains. Identify a particular act of endurance, such as making one necessary call or speaking kindly at the end of a tiring shift.

Practice. Write a request for the circumstance and a second request for the kind of strength you need within it. Put the two requests together in one prayer. Ask a trustworthy person to pray with you or provide specific support where appropriate.
Ask for strength with a particular act in view
That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, — Ephesians 3:17, KJV

Paul’s prayer joins the strengthening of the inner person to Christ dwelling in the heart by faith and to being rooted in love. Read the clauses together. The strength he asks for serves a life increasingly shaped by Christ’s presence and love. A believer seeking strength during a difficult season can ask how love should shape the next action. That might mean listening patiently, keeping an honest account, or receiving practical help without withdrawing in shame.
Scriptural testimony · Paul and Silas in prison
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them. — Acts 16:25, KJV

Read Acts 16:19–34. Paul and Silas have been beaten and imprisoned. Their prayer and singing take place before the doors open. When the jailer is in danger of harming himself, Paul calls out to preserve his life. The account keeps their suffering, their worship, and their attention to another person together. Inner strength can be visible in the way a person responds to someone who also needs help.

Bring a specific burden into prayer. Then identify one responsibility within it that you can address today. If the burden is beyond your capacity, ask a trustworthy person for a defined kind of help. You might ask someone to accompany you to a difficult meeting or take one household task for the week. Receiving that help can make it possible to fulfill the responsibility that remains yours.
Visual summary
Ask for inner strength
Depend on Christ in weakness
Practice faithful endurance
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
A week of endurance

On the first day, write the responsibility and the kind of strength you need. On the third, review what has drained your capacity and whether a practical adjustment is available. On the seventh, record where you received help and how you responded to others. Return to Paul’s prayer and give thanks for grace you might otherwise have overlooked.
Prayer. Father, strengthen me by Your Spirit in the inner person. Give me grace for the responsibility before me and teach me to receive help with gratitude. Amen.
Chapter 10 Rooted and Grounded in Love
Love takes practical shape through attention, time, and care. Consider the concrete need in front of you.

That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God. — Ephesians 3:17–19, KJV

Paul uses two pictures. Roots draw life from the soil, and a foundation gives a building stability. Both pictures ask you to consider what holds a life steady. The words “with all saints” matter. A believer can learn about Christ’s love beside other believers by worshiping, serving, bearing burdens, and hearing how others have received care. Paul asks God to give knowledge of a love that exceeds what we can fully comprehend.
Scriptural testimony · Jesus washes His disciples’ feet
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another’s feet. — John 13:14, KJV

Read John 13:1–17, 34–35. Jesus places an act of service within the disciples’ view of His authority. They are given an example they can imitate in their relationships. Consider a person whose work helps you but whose effort you rarely name. Learn what their work takes. Ask whether there is a real burden you can share, and follow through on the answer.
Love acquires a recognizable form
My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. — 1 John 3:18, KJV

Read 1 John 3:16–18. John refers to Christ laying down His life, then raises the situation of a person who has resources and sees a brother in need. The final instruction reaches both deed and truth. A helpful act should correspond to the need the person actually has. Ask before choosing the assistance, and be plain about what you can give.

The invitation in Ephesians to comprehend love “with all saints” gives this practice a community setting. You can learn something of Christ’s love when you receive care as well as when you offer it. Consider the person who quietly made a difficult week manageable. Name what they did, give thanks to God, and tell them how it helped if appropriate. That attention may also teach you how to care for someone else.
Scriptural testimony · A traveler’s need is met
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. — Luke 10:34, KJV

Read Luke 10:25–37. Jesus answers a question about the neighbor through the Samaritan’s response to the injured traveler. The story gives a sequence of actions, each addressing an immediate need. He approaches, treats the wounds, transports the traveler, and arranges continued care. Compassion reaches the practical details that allow a person to receive help beyond the first encounter.

Where a situation requires trained assistance, seek it promptly and act within your ability. In everyday care, the same attention to continuity can matter. If you bring a meal, confirm when it is needed. If you offer transport, agree how the return trip will work. If you promise to follow up, set a time. Practical details can make an expression of love dependable.
Visual summary
Rooted in Christ’s love
Understand together
Give love practical expression
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Complete the study with a commitment

Return to Ephesians 1:3, 2:10, and 3:17. Under each verse, name one gift of God or one purpose that follows it. Choose a practice for the next four weeks. You might pray Paul’s prayer for someone each week, correct one harmful habit, or commit to an act of service with the person receiving it. Plan a date to look back and ask where your understanding of Christ’s love has changed what you do.

Choose one relationship in which the teaching of Ephesians has exposed a need for change. Write what God has given in Christ, what the relationship needs, and one action you will take. Ask the other person what would make that action useful where appropriate. Review the commitment after two weeks. Record both what you did and what you learned from the person receiving it.
Prayer. Father, root and ground me in Christ’s love. Help me comprehend it with Your people and put it into practice in the relationships You have given me. Amen.
